H1.text: Ice floats on water. Water boils only at a hundred degrees. And the two strands of your D N A stay zipped together.

H2.text: Three different puzzles. One tiny pull explains all three.

H3.text: Diya sees it in her kitchen. She drops an ice cube into a glass of water.

H4.text: Most solids sink in their own liquid. But the ice floats.

H5.text: By the end, you will know why. The answer is a hydrogen bond.

P2.text: Think of a tug of war. In a bond, two atoms share a pair of electrons, like two kids holding one rope.

P3.text: If one kid is much stronger, the rope slides to that side.

P4.text: Atoms do the same. The pull an atom has on shared electrons is called electronegativity.

P5.text: The strongest pullers are fluorine, oxygen and nitrogen. F, O and N.

P6.text: Now join hydrogen to fluorine. Fluorine pulls the shared pair far away from hydrogen.

P7.text: So fluorine gets a small minus charge, and hydrogen a small plus charge. We write them delta minus and delta plus. Delta means a small part.

S1.text: Now put some H F molecules on our molecule bench.

S2.text: Plus attracts minus, like magnets. So the hydrogen of one molecule turns to the fluorine of the next.

S3.text: Fluorine also has lone pairs. A lone pair is a pair of electrons that is not shared in any bond.

S4.text: The plus hydrogen sticks to that lone pair. This pull between molecules is a hydrogen bond.

S5.text: We draw it as a dotted line. The covalent bond inside each molecule is a solid line.

S6.text: Watch. H F molecules link into a zig zag chain.

S7.text: So, a hydrogen bond needs a hydrogen joined to F, O or N, and a lone pair on a nearby F, O or N.

S8.text: It is much weaker than a covalent bond. It is strongest in solids, and weakest in gases.

V1.text: There are two kinds of hydrogen bond.

V2.text: Intermolecular means between molecules. Inter, like an inter school match, between two schools. Water, H F and alcohols do this.

V3.text: Intramolecular means inside one molecule. Intra, like a match inside one school.

V4.text: In ortho nitrophenol, the O H group and the N O two group sit side by side. So the hydrogen sits between two oxygens of the same molecule.

V5.text: In para nitrophenol, the two groups sit on opposite sides. So its hydrogen reaches out to other molecules.

B1.text: Pause and think. Which one boils at a lower temperature, ortho nitrophenol or para nitrophenol?

B2.text: Ortho! Its hydrogen bond is used up inside itself. So its molecules hold their neighbours weakly, and escape easily.

T1.text: Remember this. A hydrogen bond is a bridge. Hydrogen holds one atom by a covalent bond, and the other by a hydrogen bond.

W2.text: Which of these form hydrogen bonds? Methane, ammonia, hydrogen sulphide and methanol.

W3.text: Methane, C H four. Its hydrogens sit on carbon. Carbon is not F, O or N. So, no.

W4.text: Ammonia, N H three. Hydrogen sits on nitrogen, and nitrogen has a lone pair. Yes.

W5.text: Hydrogen sulphide, H two S. Sulphur is not a strong enough puller. So, no.

W6.text: Methanol, C H three O H. Hydrogen sits on oxygen. Yes.

W7.text: Proof: water boils at a hundred degrees Celsius. H two S, with no hydrogen bonds, boils at about minus sixty.

C2.text: In liquid water, the molecules tumble and crowd close together.

C3.text: When water freezes, each molecule locks into hydrogen bonds with four neighbours.

C4.text: These bonds hold the molecules apart, in open rings with empty space inside.

C5.text: More space, less mass in each cube. Ice is about zero point nine two grams per centimetre cube. Water is about one.

C6.text: Less dense things float. So ice floats on water. Hydrogen bonds also help alcohol mix with water, and hold D N A strands together.

X2.text: Many students say that the O H bond inside water is the hydrogen bond.

X3.text: No. That O H bond is covalent. The hydrogen bond is the weaker pull between one water molecule and the next.

E1.text: Where is this asked? J E E Main asked about ortho nitrophenol in twenty twenty one. Expect statement questions and boiling point order questions.

Q1.text: Exam level now. Which has the highest boiling point? Water, hydrogen fluoride, ammonia or hydrogen sulphide? Pause and solve.

A2.text: H two S has no hydrogen bonds. So it boils lowest.

A3.text: Fluorine pulls hardest. But H F has only one hydrogen, so it makes about two hydrogen bonds each.

A4.text: Water has two hydrogens and two lone pairs, so up to four hydrogen bonds each. More bonds, higher boiling point. B is the trap.

Y2.text: One. Hydrogen must be joined to which three atoms, to form a hydrogen bond?

Y3.text: Two. Why does ortho nitrophenol boil lower than para nitrophenol?

Y4.text: Three. Why does ice float on water?
